title: Face, Arm, Speech—and the Signs FAST Can Miss
subtitle: Additional Daily Read: A five-minute guide to recognizing possible stroke symptoms, acting promptly and remembering that a checklist cannot rule out an emergency.

body: A useful thing to know before you need it

Stroke symptoms can begin suddenly, and the person experiencing them may not be able to explain what feels wrong. A friend who recognizes a change and knows what to do can help connect that person with emergency care. This is a small piece of shared knowledge, not a request to diagnose someone or take responsibility for deciding whether a stroke is happening.

The familiar F.A.S.T. prompt helps people remember several warning signs: Face, Arm, Speech, Time. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also describes B.E. F.A.S.T., which adds Balance and Eyes. Those additions matter because a possible stroke may show up as a sudden problem walking or staying balanced, or a sudden change in vision—not only as a drooping face or unusual speech. [1]

F.A.S.T. gives you a short sequence to keep in mind. Face: look for a sudden uneven appearance, such as one side drooping. Arms: notice sudden weakness or numbness, especially on one side; a person may have trouble lifting or holding up an arm. Speech: listen for difficulty speaking or understanding, or speech that sounds unusual. Time: if you notice a possible sign, call 911 rather than waiting to see whether it passes.

The prompt is a recognition aid, not a test to administer until you get a reassuring result. You do not need to ask a person to repeat an exercise, score their responses or decide what caused the change. If something seems suddenly wrong, treat that concern as a reason to get emergency help. The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross guidelines cover first-aid treatment for critical and common medical, traumatic, environmental and toxicological conditions. [2]
Add balance and eyes to the picture

B.E. F.A.S.T. widens the reminder: Balance and Eyes join Face, Arms, Speech and Time. A sudden loss of balance, difficulty walking or a new vision problem can be easy to misread as clumsiness, tiredness or a passing inconvenience. The useful distinction here is not whether you can name the cause, but whether the change came on suddenly and could be a warning sign.

Other possible symptoms include sudden numbness or weakness, particularly on one side of the body; confusion or difficulty understanding; and a sudden severe headache. Symptoms do not have to arrive as a neat set, and someone may have one sign rather than several. Keep the categories broad in your memory: movement and balance, vision, one-sided sensation or strength, thinking and speech, and severe headache. [1]

A person who does not show the classic F.A.S.T. signs is not thereby proven safe. F.A.S.T. is designed to help recognize possible stroke signs; it is not a way to rule out a stroke. The additional Balance and Eyes prompts help cover more warning signs, but even B.E. F.A.S.T. is a reminder, not a complete diagnostic tool.

That limit is important in ordinary life. A friend might have trouble seeing clearly but speak normally. Someone else might suddenly struggle to walk without facial drooping. If a sudden symptom is concerning, do not use a normal response to one prompt to dismiss another. Nor should you wait for symptoms to become more obvious, for a second sign to appear, or for the person to feel certain. The safest action is to call 911 when stroke is suspected. [1]

Call 911 as soon as possible if sudden symptoms suggest stroke, even if they begin to improve or disappear. A symptom that fades still deserves an urgent response; waiting to see what happens can delay assessment. If you can, note the time the symptoms first appeared. That detail can help the responders and medical team understand the timeline. [1]

Do not drive the person to the hospital yourself. The American Heart Association advises calling 911 for stroke symptoms rather than self-transporting; emergency medical services can respond if the person’s condition worsens while help is on the way. [3] Tell the dispatcher plainly what changed, when it began if known, and where you are. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The goal is not to provide a diagnosis over the phone, but to get professional help moving promptly.
A five-minute learning moment for two

This can be a short conversation between friends, housemates or relatives—not a drill that tries to imitate an emergency. Spend a minute naming the letters in F.A.S.T. and the signs each one reminds you to notice. Then add Balance and Eyes: sudden trouble walking or staying steady, and sudden vision trouble. Use ordinary words rather than memorizing a medical script.

Next, agree on the central action: call 911 for sudden possible stroke symptoms, even if they fade. If the situation is real, note when the symptoms began if possible, and do not drive the person to the hospital. You can save an official CDC or NIH information page somewhere easy to find, but avoid making access to a phone or saved page a prerequisite for acting. If a sudden warning sign is happening, call first; look up details later.

Before you finish, take turns saying the plan in your own words. One person might name sudden facial drooping, one-sided arm weakness or unusual speech; the other might add a sudden balance or vision problem. Then each person says the first action: call 911. Include the two details that are easy to lose under pressure—don’t wait just because symptoms improve, and note when they began if you can. Keep this exchange calm and brief. The point is not to pass a quiz or promise that you will recognize every stroke; it is to make the next step familiar enough to use when someone needs help.
